title: Shilajit (Asphaltum): Uses, Evidence & Safety | Ayurveda
metaDescription: Shilajit: the mineral-rich Himalayan exudate used in Ayurveda, what the small studies show, and why raw shilajit's heavy-metal contamination makes testing essential.
h1: Shilajit (Asphaltum): Traditional Use, Evidence and Cautions
answerCapsule: Shilajit (śilājatu) is a sticky, mineral-rich exudate that seeps from Himalayan rocks — not a plant, but a blackish-brown resin of decomposed plant matter and minerals used in Ayurveda as a rasayana [1]. Small studies have examined its fulvic acid for energy and cognition [1]. Raw shilajit can carry heavy metals and needs purification, so tested, processed forms matter [3].

sections.capsule: Shilajit (Sanskrit शिलाजतु, IAST śilājatu; pharmacopoeial name Asphaltum) is not a herb but a mineral-organic exudate that oozes from rock crevices in the Himalayas and other high mountains during warm months. Formed over centuries from slowly decomposed plant material, it is a blackish-brown resin rich in fulvic and humic acids and trace minerals, classed in Ayurveda as a rasayana.
sections.body:
Unlike the herbs in this section, shilajit is not botanical at all — it is an *exudate*, a tar-like substance that seeps from rocks in mountain ranges including the Himalayas, Altai, Caucasus and Andes. Analyses describe it as the product of centuries of microbial breakdown of plant matter compressed within rock, leaving a complex of fulvic acid, humic substances and dozens of trace minerals [1].

In Ayurveda shilajit is a celebrated *rasayana*, traditionally described as *yogavahi* (a carrier said to enhance other medicines) and used as a tonic for stamina and vigour, especially where [vata or kapha](/doshas) is involved [2]. Classical practice is emphatic that raw shilajit must undergo *śodhana* — a purification step — before use, a traditional instinct that modern contamination testing has since given a concrete reason for. Genuine shilajit is also widely adulterated, so provenance matters.

sections.h2: What does the science say about shilajit?
sections.capsule: Shilajit has a thin human evidence base. Laboratory work centres on fulvic acid, which researchers have studied as an antioxidant and for its effect on proteins involved in memory [1]. A few small human trials have looked at fatigue, male fertility and altitude stress, but they are limited in size and quality, so shilajit is studied for these uses rather than proven to work [2].
sections.body:
The scientific reality is modest. Most laboratory interest focuses on fulvic acid, shilajit's main active fraction, studied for antioxidant activity and, in preclinical work, for an effect on the aggregation of tau — a protein linked to Alzheimer's disease — which is why some reviews frame it as of *potential* interest for cognition [1]. That is a laboratory hypothesis, not a demonstrated benefit in people.

Human studies exist but are few and small: short trials have reported changes in testosterone in men, in markers of tiredness, and in adaptation to high altitude, and independent reviewers judge the overall bioactivity to lack substantial evidence [2]. The honest summary is that shilajit is an interesting, mineral-rich substance whose traditional reputation far exceeds what controlled research has so far confirmed. See [Is Ayurveda scientific?](/is-ayurveda-scientific) and the [panchakarma](/panchakarma) pages for how such claims are weighed.

sections.h2: What are the side effects and cautions of shilajit?
sections.capsule: Shilajit's main safety issue is not the substance itself but what raw material can carry: reviews report it contains many heavy metals, and unpurified or poorly processed shilajit can hold unsafe levels of lead, arsenic, mercury, mycotoxins and fungi [3]. Purified, laboratory-tested forms are essential. Avoid shilajit in pregnancy, with haemochromatosis or gout, and if you take medicines it might interact with.
sections.body:
The specific cautions:

- **Heavy metals and contamination:** the dominant concern. Because shilajit forms inside rock, it naturally concentrates minerals — including toxic ones — and reviews note it can contain dozens of heavy metals; raw or crudely processed material can also carry mycotoxins and fungi [3]. Only buy shilajit that has been purified and independently tested, with a certificate of analysis for lead, arsenic, mercury and cadmium.
- **Iron overload:** shilajit contains iron and humic substances, so it is best avoided if you have haemochromatosis or any iron-overload condition.
- **Gout:** its mineral content may raise uric acid in susceptible people, a theoretical concern in gout.
- **Pregnancy and breastfeeding:** safety is not established; avoid.
- **Medicine interactions:** because it may affect iron levels, blood sugar and blood pressure, take care alongside relevant medicines and tell your doctor.
- **Adulteration:** cheap shilajit is frequently faked or bulked out; a suspiciously low price is a red flag for quality, and quality is the whole safety story here [4].

The wider heavy-metal problem across Ayurvedic products sold online is well documented, which is exactly why third-party testing — not the word 'natural' — is what makes shilajit safe to consider [4].

sections.h2: Where can I find quality shilajit?
sections.capsule: Shilajit is one product where sourcing is the entire safety question, because contamination lives in the raw material rather than the idea. Choose purified shilajit from a maker that follows a recognised Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standard and publishes third-party heavy-metal testing [4]. Where shilajit is used within care, it is prescribed and monitored by a physician at an NABH-accredited Ayurvedic hospital, not bought on price alone.
sections.body:
Purified shilajit made to a recognised **Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standard**, with a published certificate of analysis showing heavy metals below safe limits, is the only responsible way to use it — the difference between a tested extract and raw mountain resin is a difference in safety, not marketing [4]. That is a statement about quality control, not a claim that shilajit treats any condition.

Because genuine shilajit is costly and heavily adulterated, provenance and testing matter more here than for almost any other Ayurvedic product. If you are considering it, do so through a qualified Ayurvedic physician who can check it against your health and medicines. Compare it with the herbs in this cluster — [ashwagandha](/herbs/ashwagandha), [guduchi](/herbs/guduchi) and [triphala](/herbs/triphala) — and see the [herbs hub](/herbs) for how sourcing is assessed.

faqs.q: Is shilajit a plant or a herb?
faqs.a: No. Shilajit is not a plant or a herb but a mineral-organic exudate — a resin that seeps from rocks in the Himalayas and other mountains, formed over centuries from decomposed plant matter compressed within rock. It is rich in fulvic acid and trace minerals, and Ayurveda classes it as a rasayana.

faqs.q: Is raw shilajit safe to eat?
faqs.a: Raw, unpurified shilajit is not recommended. Reviews report it can contain heavy metals such as lead, arsenic and mercury, along with mycotoxins and fungi [3]. Ayurveda has always required a purification step, and modern practice adds laboratory testing. Only use shilajit that has been purified and independently tested for contaminants.

faqs.q: What does shilajit do, according to research?
faqs.a: Research on shilajit is early and limited. Laboratory studies focus on its fulvic acid as an antioxidant and, in preclinical models, its effect on a memory-related protein [1]; small human trials have examined fatigue, testosterone and altitude adaptation without firm conclusions [2]. It is best seen as studied for these uses, not proven to work.

faqs.q: How can I tell if shilajit is genuine and safe?
faqs.a: Genuine, safe shilajit is purified, made to a recognised Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standard, and sold with a third-party certificate of analysis confirming heavy metals are below safe limits [4]. Be wary of very cheap products and vague 'pure Himalayan' marketing without test data, since adulteration and contamination are common.
